concepts.title: When Optical Flow and Motion Flow Are Not the Same
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow and physical motion flow can differ when image brightness changes do not correspond to the actual movement of 3D points in a scene.
concepts.content:
There are a number of scenarios where motion in the image brightness does not correspond to the motion of the 3D points in the scene. Examples where the definition of motion is unclear include:

- A rotating Lambertian sphere with static illumination produces no image changes, while a static sphere with a moving light source produces perceived motion.
- Moving in front of a textureless wall produces no change in the image.
- Waves in water appear to move along the surface, but the actual motion of the water is primarily up and down.
- A rotating mirror or any surface with a specular component will produce the appearance of faster motion.
- A camera moving in front of a specular planar surface will not produce a motion field corresponding to a homography.

Ideally, motion estimation should assign the physical cause to each source of variation in the image, rather than just measuring pixel motion.
concepts.motivation_md: In computer vision, we often assume that changes in pixel intensity represent physical movement. However, lighting changes, reflections, and lack of texture can create 'optical flow' that does not match the actual 'motion field' of objects, necessitating a distinction between the two.
concepts.recap_md: - Optical flow is the apparent motion of brightness patterns, while motion flow is the actual 3D movement of scene points.

concepts.title: The Aperture Problem
concepts.one_liner: The aperture problem occurs when observing a 1D structure through a limited window, making it impossible to determine the true motion direction.
concepts.content:
One classical example of the limitations of motion estimation from images is the aperture problem. The aperture problem happens when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame, as shown in (see figure: Aperture problem when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame. The actual motion of the bar is upward, but the perception, when vision is limited to what...). If none of the termination points are in view within the observation window (i.e., the aperture), it is impossible to measure the actual image motion. Only the component orthogonal to the moving structure can be measured.

The Barber-pole illusion is an illustration of the aperture problem. The barber pole induces the illusion of downward motion while rotating.

concepts.title: Representation of Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Motion can be represented either as dense optical flow images or as a sparse set of moving point tracks.
concepts.content:
Motion over time can be modeled as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) ight]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$ and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. A limitation of this formulation is the lack of an explicit representation of the trajectory followed by specific scene points over time, as a location $(x,y)$ may correspond to different scene elements as time changes.

An alternative representation is to model motion as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): $$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$ This requires establishing the correspondence of the same scene point over time (tracking). This can be challenging because the appearance of a 3D point changes due to perspective projection and illumination variations. Consequently, most point-based representations use a sparse set rather than a dense array.

Choosing between these representations depends on the application, and for complex flows like smoke or water, the ideal representation remains an open question.
concepts.motivation_md: Different computer vision tasks require different ways of describing motion; dense flow is useful for video compression or stabilization, while sparse tracks are better for 3D reconstruction and object tracking.
concepts.recap_md: - Dense optical flow assigns a velocity vector to every pixel in the image.

concepts.title: Brightness Constancy Assumption
concepts.one_liner: The brightness constancy assumption states that the captured brightness of a scene element remains constant as it moves.
concepts.content:
The brightness constancy assumption says that as a scene element moves in the world, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time. Mathematically, this assumption translates into the following relationship, given a sequence $\ell(x,y,t)$:

$$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  = \ell(x,y,t)$$

where $u$ and $v$ are the element displacement over one unit of time and are functions of pixel location $u(x,y)$ and $v(x,y)$. This is equivalent to saying that $\ell(x, y, t + 1) = \ell(x-u,y-v,t)$. (see figure: Translation to the right of a simple $6 \times 6$ size image.)

The constant brightness assumption only approximately holds in reality. For it to be exact, the scene should have Lambertian objects illuminated from a light source at infinity, with no occlusions, shadows, or interreflections. In reality, pixels might be occluded in one frame or new pixels might appear at boundaries and behind occlusions.
concepts.motivation_md: This assumption provides the fundamental constraint needed to solve for motion: it links the spatial gradients of an image to its temporal changes, allowing us to estimate velocity.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes $\ell(x + u, y + v, t + 1) = \ell(x, y, t)$ for moving scene elements.

concepts.title: Layer-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Layer-based motion estimation represents the 2D motion field as a collection of superimposed layers, each containing a rigid object with its own motion parameters.
concepts.content: Layer-based motion estimation incorporates knowledge of 3D scene projection by assuming the scene is composed of rigid objects. In this framework, the 2D motion field is represented as a collection of superimposed layers, where each layer contains one object and occludes the layers below. Each layer is described by a different set of motion parameters. This parametric motion field can be integrated into a gradient-based approach, where motion parameters are estimated iteratively using an expectation-maximization (EM) style algorithm. At each step, the algorithm estimates which layer a pixel likely belongs to and then refines the motion parameters for each layer.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard motion estimation often ignores the 3D structure of a scene. By assuming a scene consists of rigid objects, we can use layers to better model occlusions and the specific parametric forms of motion that occur when rigid bodies move and rotate.

concepts.title: Importance of Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Motion estimation is a key attribute in image processing and computer vision for understanding scene dynamics and 3D structure.
concepts.content: Motion estimation is an important task in image processing and computer vision, used in applications such as video denoising and compression. It serves as a key attribute for understanding scene dynamics and 3D structure. Despite extensive study, achieving accurate optical flow remains challenging, even with state-of-the-art deep-learning techniques. Traditional approaches that require no training are particularly useful when exploring unsupervised learning methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Motion estimation is fundamental for high-level tasks like scene understanding and low-level tasks like video compression, providing the necessary data to interpret how objects and structures move through time.
concepts.recap_md: - Essential for video compression, denoising, and understanding 3D scene dynamics.

concepts.title: Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow is an approximation of the 2D motion field calculated by measuring the displacement of image brightness between frames.
concepts.content:
Optical flow approximates the 2D motion field by measuring the displacement of image brightness. Given two images $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$, the optical flow $[\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}]$ indicates the relative position of each pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ to its corresponding pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_2$. This definition assumes a one-to-one mapping between frames and that a single motion explains all brightness changes. These assumptions may fail during occlusions, when objects appear/disappear, or when illumination changes.

(see figure: Two frames of a sequence, ground-truth optical flow (color coded), and the color code to read the vector at each pixel.)
concepts.motivation_md: While the motion field is a purely geometric concept, optical flow is the practical method used to estimate that motion from actual pixel data in video sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - Optical flow measures the apparent motion of brightness patterns between consecutive frames.

key_passage.text: Optical flow is an approximation to the 2D motion field computed by measuring displacement of image brightness. The ideal optical flow is defined as follows: given two images ℓ₁ and ℓ₂ ∈ ℝ^(N × M × 3), the optical flow [u, v] ∈ ℝ^(N × M × 2) indicates the relative position of each pixel in ℓ₁ and the corresponding pixel in ℓ₂.

concepts.title: Gradient-Based Optical Flow Estimation (Lucas-Kanade)
concepts.one_liner: The Lucas-Kanade method estimates optical flow by solving a system of linear equations derived from the gradient constraint and local spatial consistency.
concepts.content: The Lucas-Kanade method approximates the change between consecutive frames using a first-order Taylor expansion. Combined with the brightness constancy assumption, this yields the **gradient constraint equation**: $u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$. This equation alone is insufficient to determine motion (the aperture problem), so the method assumes motion is constant over a local image patch. By minimizing a weighted sum of squared constraints over a neighborhood using a Gaussian window $g(x,y)$, we solve for $(u,v)$: $$\mathcal{L}(u, v) = \sum g \left| u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t \right| ^2$$ Setting derivatives with respect to $u$ and $v$ to zero leads to a $2 \times 2$ system at each location: $$\begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x ^ 2  & \sum g \ell_x \ell_y \\ \sum g \ell_x \ell_y & \sum g \ell_y ^ 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = - \begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x \ell_t \\ \sum g \ell_y \ell_t \end{bmatrix}$$ The matrix $\mathbf{A}$ must be invertible for a unique solution, which fails in regions with 1D structure. (see figure: Gradient-based optical flow estimation using two input frames.) (see figure: Toy sequence with two moving squares. The red arrows indicate the direction of motion of each square.) (see figure: Estimated optical flow in the regions with $R > 2$ (around *good features to track* @shi1994goodfeatures)

concepts.title: Gradient Constraint Equation
concepts.one_liner: The gradient constraint equation relates image motion to spatial and temporal derivatives, defining a line of possible motion vectors perpendicular to the image gradient.
concepts.content: The **gradient constraint equation** is defined as: $$u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$$ This equation constrains the motion $(u,v)$ in location $(x,y)$ to be along a line perpendicular to the image gradient $\nabla \ell= \left( \ell_x, \ell_y \right)$ at that location. This is the same relationship that appears when describing the aperture problem, where local motion cannot be uniquely determined from a single point.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a fundamental mathematical link between observable intensity changes and the underlying velocity field, though it only constrains motion in one dimension locally.
concepts.recap_md: - Relates spatial and temporal image derivatives to the velocity components $u$ and $v$. - Constrains motion to a line perpendicular to the local image gradient, leading to the aperture problem.

concepts.title: Iterative Refinement for Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Iterative refinement improves optical flow accuracy by minimizing photometric reconstruction error through successive warping and multiscale Gaussian pyramids.
concepts.content: Iterative refinement improves motion estimation by directly minimizing the **photometric reconstruction** error: $$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$ Unlike the single-step gradient method, this approach uses gradient descent to iteratively update the flow $(u, v)$. At each iteration $n$, the current estimate is used to compute a warped frame $\ell_1 (x+u_n,y+v_n,t+1)$, and an update $(\Delta u_n, \Delta v_n)$ is computed. To handle large displacements, this is performed across a Gaussian pyramid, starting from the lowest resolution and upsampling the result to initialize the next level. (see figure: Multiscale iterative refinement for optical flow. Optical flow estimation is done on a Gaussian pyramid.) (see figure: Comparison between the optical flow estimated using the gradient-based algorithm and the multiscale iterative refinement approach.) Regularization terms can be added to the objective, such as the Horn-Schunck formulation: $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) + \lambda R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard gradient methods fail when motion is large; iterative refinement and pyramids allow for accurate estimation of significant displacements by linearizing the problem at multiple scales.
concepts.recap_md: - Minimizes photometric reconstruction error directly using gradient descent and iterative warping. - Employs a Gaussian pyramid to estimate large motions at coarse scales before refining at finer scales. - Can incorporate regularization terms like the Horn-Schunck objective to enforce smoothness.

key_passage.text: At each iteration n, the estimated optical flow will be used to compute the warped frame ℓ1(x+un,y+vn,t+1) and we will compute an update, Δun and Δvn, of the optical flow: un+1 = un+Δun and vn+1= vn + Δvn. To improve the results, the optical flow estimation is done on a Gaussian pyramid.

concepts.title: Photometric Reconstruction Error
concepts.one_liner: Photometric reconstruction error measures the squared difference between a reference frame and a warped subsequent frame to evaluate motion estimation.
concepts.content: The **photometric reconstruction** error is a loss function that measures the difference between a reference frame and a warped version of the subsequent frame: $$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: It serves as a direct measure of how well a motion field aligns two images, acting as the primary objective for optimization and unsupervised learning in optical flow.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures the squared difference between a reference frame and a warped subsequent frame. - Acts as a data-fidelity term in optical flow optimization and unsupervised learning.

concepts.title: Horn-Schunck Objective
concepts.one_liner: The Horn-Schunck objective combines photometric reconstruction error with a regularization term to estimate a smooth and consistent optical flow field.
concepts.content: The Horn-Schunck objective incorporates a regularization term penalizing fast variations on the estimated optical flow: $$ \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) + \lambda R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) $$ This problem formulation was introduced by Horn and Schunck in 1981.
concepts.motivation_md: It addresses the ill-posed nature of the optical flow problem by introducing global constraints, ensuring the resulting motion field is physically plausible and smooth.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines photometric reconstruction error with a regularization term $R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$. - Uses a parameter $\lambda$ to balance matching accuracy with the smoothness of the flow field.

concepts.title: Slow Prior
concepts.one_liner: The slow prior is a regularization term that penalizes large velocity magnitudes to favor smaller motion estimates.
concepts.content: The **slow prior** is a regularization term that penalizes large velocities in the estimated optical flow field: $$ R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{x,y} \left( u(x,y) \right)^2 + \left( v(x,y)  \right)^2 $$
concepts.motivation_md: It helps resolve ambiguities in motion estimation by assuming that, in the absence of strong evidence, scene elements are likely to be stationary or moving slowly.
concepts.recap_md: - Penalizes the magnitude of velocity vectors to favor smaller motion estimates. - Helps resolve ambiguities by assuming scene elements are likely to move slowly.

concepts.title: Smooth Prior
concepts.one_liner: The smooth prior is a regularization term that penalizes spatial variations in the optical flow field to encourage neighboring pixels to move similarly.
concepts.content: The **smooth prior** is a regularization term that penalizes spatial variations in the optical flow field, encouraging neighboring pixels to have similar motion: $$R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{x,y} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}  \right)^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: It enforces the physical intuition that objects are generally coherent, meaning adjacent pixels on the same object should have nearly identical motion vectors.
concepts.recap_md: - Penalizes spatial derivatives of the optical flow to encourage neighboring pixels to move similarly. - Models the physical coherence of objects to produce a less noisy motion field.

prereq.rationale: The text identifies the pursuit of accurate optical flow as the central challenge within the broader task of motion estimation.
This concept explores the limitations of the optical flow definition by showing cases where brightness changes do not match physical motion.
The aperture problem describes a fundamental ambiguity in measuring optical flow when observing 1D structures through a limited window.
Once optical flow is defined, it can be represented in different ways, such as dense fields or sparse tracks.
Lucas-Kanade uses the brightness constancy assumption to formulate the motion estimation problem.
Lucas-Kanade solves the aperture problem by assuming motion is constant over a local spatial neighborhood.
The gradient constraint equation is derived by applying a first-order Taylor expansion to the brightness constancy assumption.
The photometric error is a direct mathematical implementation of the brightness constancy assumption.
The Horn-Schunck method uses the photometric reconstruction error as its data term.
Layer-based estimation typically uses gradient-based optimization to refine the motion parameters of each layer.

overlay.rationale: This definition formalizes the conceptual ambiguity described in the aperture problem.
The barber-pole illusion is a classic visual phenomenon that illustrates the aperture problem.
Dense optical flow is a specific representation where motion is modeled as a velocity vector for every pixel.
A sparse set of moving points is an alternative representation that focuses on tracking specific scene elements.
Sparse tracks provide explicit trajectories of scene points over time, addressing a key limitation of dense optical flow.
The mathematical relationship $\ell(x+u, y+v, t+1) = \ell(x,y,t)$ formalizes the conceptual assumption.
Iterative refinement builds upon the principles of gradient-based flow but uses warping to handle larger displacements.
